Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court (Mahbubey Alam, Advocate, Supreme Court, with him), instructed by Syed Sakhawat Ali, Advocate on Record -----For the Appellant,
M.H. Khondker, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by S R. Karmakar, Advocate on Record -----For the Respondent No. 1.

S.M. Basiruddin ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.—This appeal by special leave arises from an application under section 14 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 filed by respondent No. l in respect of certain land with the Dacca City. The sale under pre-emption was effected by Ayesha Khatun respondent No. 2 in favour of the appellant by a kabala dated 10-9-73 which was registered on 5-4-76. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 214 under Mouza Shahar Dacca, owned by Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik, and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got 1/3rd share and Ran-gubala got the remaining rd share. One Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik by a registered deed of sale dated 19-7-52 became co-sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala created a lease in respect of her 2/3rd share for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 in favour of Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2 Nafisa Khatun sold her interest to respondent No. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 18-4-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 10-9-73. Against this sale respondent No. 1 filed the application for pre-emption. The appellant contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was not a co-sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani ; and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun by Rangubala by granting permanent lease for 99 years, reserving for herself annual rent of Tk. 1/-; and that Ayesha Khatun paid rent of Tk. 1/- to the lessor Rangubala till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government; and that S.A. Khatian was not correctly prepared because neither respondent No. 1 nor his vendor was co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun. He further claimed that after his purchase he applied for mutation of his name and accordingly his name was mutated in the S A. Khatian and jama was separated. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed pre-emption case against the appellant and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court Division in revision under section 115(1)1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and being unsuccessful moved this Court and obtained leave from this Court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court Division. 

 2. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division was correct in making no distinction between the expression 'holding' as occurring in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the expression 'non-agricultural land' as occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. At the hearing of the appeal the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant made two points out of the leave order. Firstly, he argued that upgradation of an under tenant to the status of a tenant under the Government on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest over the tenant by the notification in April, 1956 did not have the effect of merging the two distinct interests, that is, of Akshoy and Rangubala on one side and that of Ayesha Khatun on the other hand; and, according to the learned Advocate, Ayesha Khatun attained the status of full tenant on up gradation and ceased to be a co-sharer-tenant of successor-in-interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik. In this context, he alternatively argued that the shares of Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala having been partitioned by the decree of the civil court in partition suit, resulting in the creation of two separate holdings under the Municipality. Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala ceased to be co-sharer in the tenancy. Secondly he argued that the expression 'non-agricultural land' as occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act not being expression 'holding' as occurring in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the learned Judge of the High Court Division fell into an error in treating the successors-in interest of Akshoy Kumar Saba Banik as co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun, and allowing the pre-emption case. In this connection the learned Advocate submitted that the decision relied upon by the High Court Division in the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury v. Mosammat Rezia Begum, (l964) 16 DLR 77 has not laid down the law on correct interpretation of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 3. Now let me examine the first point argued by Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant The learned Advocate strenuously argued in support of the proposition that on the elimination of the rent-receiving interest the under raiyati interest of Ayesha Khatun by operation of law became upgraded and attained the independent status of raiyat under the Government. On careful consideration of the argument of the learned Advocate I find it difficult to accept his proposition. Chapter IV of Part IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for "preparation of record-of-rights." This chapter contains the provision of preparation of record of rights with a view to assessment of compensation regarding interests of all rent-receivers which are liable to be acquired and which have already been acquired under Chapter II of the Act. Section 17 empowers the Government to make an order for preparation of record-of-rights. Section 18 provides that the Revenue-officers are to record certain particulars in the record of rights. Section 19 provides that they are to prepare the draft as well as final publication of such records. Section 20 prescribed the quantum of land 'which can be retained' by a person in his possession. Sections 21 and 22 provide that all lands are subject to payment of fair and equitable rent, as determined by the Revenue-officer in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV and the rent so determined shall be entered in the record-of-rights. Sections 23 to 28 require the Revenue-officers to assess fair and equitable rents for different classes of tenants. Section 29 provides that the rents entered in the record-of-rights shall be deemed to have been correctly determined and to be fair and equitable. Preparation of record-of-rights in a district, part of a district or local area as provided in section 17 was intended to- 

 (k) the special conditions and incidents, if any, of the tenancy; 

 4. According to section 18 the Revenue-officer is required to prepare or revise the record-of-rights in pursuance of the order passed under section 17, and in preparing or revising the record-of-eights the Revenue- officer has been directed to record such particulars as may be prescribed under the Rules. Rule 18 quoted above shows that the nature of the particulars to be recorded as provided in clause (b) of rule 18 the Revenue officer is required to record the class or the classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, whether the tenant is a proprietor, tenure holder, raiyat holding at fixed rates, settled raiyar, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy raiyat, under raiyat, with or without a right of occupancy, or a non-agricultural tenant, and if he is a tenure-holder, whether be is a permanent tenure-bolder or not, and whether his rent is liable to enhancement during the continuance of his tenure, Clause (f) requires that rent payable at the time the record-of-rights is being prepared as well as the rents determined as fair and equitable according to rules 28 to 30 to be mentioned. Rule 24 provides for preparation of preliminary record-of-rights which is also known as draft record-or-rights. According to this rule, the draft record shall consist of statements of rights which are styled as the khatians. This rule further directs that ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested, or each group of persons jointly interested, in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyar, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons. Statutory provisions clearly show sections 18 and 19 and the rules 18, 19 and 24 do not support the proposition canvassed by the learned Advocate on the elimination of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats became raiyats under the Government and their status having thus been upgraded, the Revenue-officer while preparing the record-ofrights was required to record the under-raiyat as a raiyat in separate khatian, fixing fair and equitable rent for such upgraded tenant. It has already been stated above that the preparation of record of rights as provided in section 17 was with a view to assessment of compensation payable for all such interests liable to be acquired under the Act. Rule 24 provides for preparation of statements of rights which is styled as the khatian. According to this rule ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested or each group of persons jointly interested in the land whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, according to particulars mentioned in rule 18. The rules neither authorize nor require the Revenue-officer to prepare separate khatians for the individual raiyats and under-raysts, but, on the other hand, it provides that each group of person jointly interested in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant ordinarily are to be shown in separate khatian, and it further provides that each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, recording the particulars as indicated in rule 18. In support of the proposition that the under raiyat was upgraded to the status of raiyat, on the elimination of rent receiving interest, support was sought from the doctrine of merger as provide in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which provides that when the raiyati disappears the under-raiyat cannot any longer remain as such. Section 22 as it stands after amendment of 1907 merely provides that 08 the transfer of the occupancy right to a person jointly interested in the land as proprietor or permanent tenure-holder, such person shall have no right to hold the land as the raiyat but shall hold it as a proprietor or permanent tenure-holder as the case may be. By the amendment of 1907 the principle of merger as contemplated in section 22 was altered. The most important incident of merger under sub-section (1) of section 22 is that the landlord does not hold the land upon merger as a raiyat but holds it only as a proprietor or a permanent tenure-holder. It necessarily follows that the under-raiyats are automatically promoted to the status of raiyats. This view received judicial recognition in Ram Charan Sutradhar Vs. SM. Makhan, 38 CWN 1976, and it was followed by a Division Bench in the case of Pramatha Nath Shikder Vs. Jitendra Nath Roy. 43 CWN 1102. Upon acquisition of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats by operation of law became raiyats under the Government is not in controversy, but the doctrine of merger as provided in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has no application to the conversion of all tenants holding land as proprietor, tenure holder raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant, as raiyats or maliks under the Government. 

 5. The question boils down to this, whether on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest, that is, the interest of Akshoy and Rangubala Choudhurani the under-raiyati created by the latter by executing permanent lease dated 23-12-63 for 99 years in favour of Ayesha Khatun, respondent No.2, stood upgraded to that of a raiyat and the statute recognizes the upgraded under-raiyat as raiyat for all practical purposes. The khatian was rightly prepared in accordance with rule 18, recording the under-raiyat of Ayesha Khatun without changing its status. Rule 18 provides that while preparing the record-of-right the Revenue-officer concerned shall record the class or classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, that is, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy-raiyat, under raiyat, etc. There is nothing in rule 18, which requires the Revenue-officer to record the under-raiyat as the upgraded raiyat in the khatian. It is in evidence that the S. A. Khatian was prepared by the Revenue-officer under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act recording Akshoy Kumar Saba Banik and Rangubala Cboudhurani as raiyats and Ayesha Khatun as under raiyat, and Jama of Tk. 10/- fixed under the Bengal Tenancy Act remaining the same. According to Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, in the S. A. Khatian prepared after the whole sale acquisition of rent-receiving interests Rangubala Choudhuraoi could not be shown as a raiyat in the khatian, and the khatian showing Rangubala Choudhurani as a raiyat was wrong According to him. Ayesha Khatun should have been shown as a raiyat. In support of his argument reliance was placed on a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Mubasher Ali V. Md. Mokbul Hossain, 19 DLR 271 The decision seems to support the argument. The learned Judges expressed their view regarding consequential effect upon existing tenants on the acquisition of all rent-receiving interests under section 3 of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act in the following term: 

 In the reported case of course, the pre-emption case was under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act which was contested on the ground that the land purchased by the pre-emptees appertained to an under-raiyati holding created by registered kabuliyat dated 10th October, 1947 in favour of their vendor Moslemuddin; and as such the petitioner not being a co- sharer in the under-raiyati holding could not maintain the pre-emption case. Pre-emptor relied upon the doctrine of merger and upgradation of under raiyati on the elimination of the rent receiving interest over the vendor Moslemuddin. Pre-emption case was allowed by the trial Court and it was affirmed by the lower Appel1ate Court Opposite parties moved the High Court and rule was issued At the hearing of the rule it was argued that in view of the fact that all rent-receiving interests have been acquired by the Government on and from 14th April, 1956. Moslemuddin who was an under-raiyat, became a tenant direct under the Government and was therefore automatically elevated to the status of an occupancy raiyat, and that being the position in law Moslemuddin status in the under raiyati was upgraded, and consequently the petitioner became a co-sharer in the holding and therefore rightly claimed pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In answer to this contention it was argued that until final acquisition took place on the publication of tile compensation assessment roll under section 43(2) of the Act all rent-receiving interests no doubt vested in the Government but that was more or less a national vesting, because, until Part V came into operation and the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed, "One class of holders of agricultural land" that is, one class of tenants (Malik's) as provided in section 81 did not come into being. It was argued that the different' provisions of the statute show that even after the general notification of 2nd April. 1956 and the consequent, vesting of all rent receiving interests in the Government, the different classes of tenancies recognized under the Bengal Tenancy Act continued, because continuation of different classes of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act was necessary for the purpose of assessment of compensation and calculation of rate (If compensation to be paid to tenants of different classes. It was also submitted that after all these steps including the final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 43(2) of the Act, actual vesting of the different interests in the Government, as provided under section 44 of the Act, took place. 

 6. It appears from the decision that the argument made on behalf of the pre-emptee did not make any impression on the learned Judges. The learned Judges following the doctrine of merger as contained in sec. 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act expressed the opinion that in that case the raiyati interest in view of creation of under-raiyati under it, was a rent receiving interest within the meaning of the Act; and once raiyati interest (rent receiving interest) vested in the Government which became the proprietos, and consequently there being a merger of the former in the latter the under raiyati automatically stood upgraded to a raiyati. The learned Judges further observed that if an under raiyat become a tenant direct under the Proprietor, be becomes a raiyat as his landlord who was araiyat disappeared from the scene. 

 7. On carefully examining the different sections of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder, I am of the opinion that it is not correct to say that on the publication of the Notifications under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act existing classification and gradation of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared and there was only one class of tenants with effect from April 14, 1956. It is correct that with from that date all tenants irrespective of their status under the Bengal Tenancy Act became liable to pay rent direct to the Government end for that purpose alone they were treated as raiyats under the Government, but for all other purposes the tenancies continued to be regulated by the Bengal Tenancy Act, that is why the Bengal Tenancy Act was kept in force till Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation on the publication of the Notification under section 79 of the Act and Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed by operation of section 80 of the Act. In the case of Mobasher Ali V. Md. Makbul Hossain, the conclusions arrived at by learned Judges are not based on correct appreciation of the different provisions of the statute. The learned Judges applied the doctrine of merger as provided is section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which in my opinion is not applicable in the case of acquisition of rent receiving interests under section 3 of the Act. And on this wrong premise the learned Judges held that on the elimination of rent receiving interests an under-raiyat stood upgraded to the status of raiyat. It is by operation of section 3(4)(e) all tenants became tenant. directly under the Government, and as such all tenants became tenants under the Government not by a process of up gradation in consequence of merger as provided under section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Government by several Notifications acquired the interests of some of the rent- receivers as shown in the Notifications; and then by a general Notification dated the 2nd April, 1956 under section 3, acquired all the interests of the remaining rent-receivers with effect from 14th April, 1956. According to clause (e) of sub-section (4) of section 3 all tenants holding lands in such estatestaluks tenures, holdings or tenancies directly under the rent-receiver specified in Notification under sub-section (1) shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent-paying lands so held by them to the Government and not to anybody else provided that in cases where no notification was issued under sub-section (2) of section 43 before commencement of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1957, declaring that Compensation Assessment-roll in respect of the interest of any such rent-receiver in any such estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy directly under such rent-receiver, shall as the tenants under the Government, be liable to pay rents in respect of lands so held by them except rent-free lands, at the rates determined in the record of rights finally published under sub-section (3) of section 19 subject to modification under section 53. Sub-section (4), clause e) of section 3 clearly shows that purpose of this provision is to ensure collection of rent by the Government from all the tenants who were liable to pay rent to the rent- receivers before the Notification. So the mandate is that on the vesting of the receiving interests in the Government, all tenants under the rent- receivers shall be liable to pay rent direct to the Government and not to anybody else. The statutory provisions sufficiently indicate that only for the purpose of collection of rent the existing tenants became one class, that is, 'raiyats' under the Government. However, the classification and gradation of different tenancies, for all other purposes, such as, identification and determinant of their status and their rights and other liabilities, continued till the notification under sub- section (21 of section 43 was issued. Section 33 provides for preparation of Compensation Assessment roll after the publication of the record-of-rights. Section 40 provides for preliminary publication of Compensation Assessment-roll after the amount of compensation has been determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 37, 38-39. Section 42 speaks about final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll after all objections and appeals under section 40 have been disposed of. Sub-section (2) of section 43 provides that after the final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 42 in respect of any village or villages or local area, the Government shall by notification declare that a Compensation Assessment-rolls have been finally published. Section 44 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in Chapter II of this Act or in any contract, but subject to the provisions of clauses (a), (b), (c) and (d) of sub-section (4) of section 3 and Sub-section (3) of section 46E on the publication of the notification in the Official Gazette under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that the Compensation Assessment-roll has been finally published, the following amongst other consequences shall ensue, namely- 

 (2) each proprietor,  tenure-holder and other rent-receiver, whose interests in any estate, tenure Of holding or tenancy or in any part of any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy, as the case may be, within the area to which  such roll relates, are acquired under this Act, shall with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the Official Gazette, be entitled to retain possession of and hold, subject to the provisions of this Act, as a tenant directly under the Government, all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession under Chapter IV and be liable to pay rent for such lands to the Provincial Government: 

 9. The scheme of the Act as shown from the different chapters does not provide that on the publication of the Notification under section 3 all rent-receivers were eliminated and all raiyats, under raiyats non-agricultural tenants, etc. existing in the estates acquired stood upgraded and along with it classification of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared. What as a matter of fact happened is that with the publication of the Notification under section 3 all the rent receiving interests no doubts stood acquired, and the raiyats, under raiyats, non- agricultural tenants, for the purpose of payment of rent to the Government, became 'raiyats' under the Government, but the existing classification of tenants as contemplated under the Bengal Tenancy Act, and record-of-rights prepared under the Bengal Tenancy Act continued until publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 43; and the consequences as provided under section 44 ensued, namely, acquisition and vesting of the interests of proprietors, tenure-holders and other rent-receivers, absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances subject to the rights of such proprietors tenure-holders and other relit receivers specified in clause (2) of section 44. This view also gets support from the fact that Bengal Tenancy Act continued to be operative side by side with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and this state continued till commencement of Part V of the Act and the consequent repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act. 1885. Until repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act the classification of tenants, for the purpose of determination of the tenant rights and liabilities continued to be governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act otherwise there was no necessity of keeping the Bengal Tenancy Act operative along with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In view of the position in law is obtaining due to both the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Bengal Tenancy Act bolding the same field, an under ralyat, no doubt, on the elimination of the rent-receiver (raiyat who created the under raiyat) attained the status of raiyat directly under the Government, as the Government by operation of law became the owner, and the under raiyat became liable to pay rent direct to the Government and to no other agency unless specifically authorized by the Government in this behalf. In my opinion in Mobasher Ali Vs. Md. Makbul Hossain, the learned Judges were not correct in taking the view that once the raiyati interest vested in the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior interests, by the process of merger the under-raiyati automatically stood upgraded to a raiyat for all purposes. Correct analysis or the different provisions of the Act keeping in view the whole scheme of acquisition by the State of the interests of rent-receivers and certain other interests in" land in Bangladesh, does not warrant the following conclusion- 

 10. Sub-section (1) of-section 24 and section 46A read together how that an under-raiyat holding would continue to be in existence at the time of preparation of the record-of-rights which must be subsequent to the notification of 2nd April, 1956. Rule 18 of the East Bengal State Acquisition Rules, provides the particular to be recorded in the record-of- rights prepared under section 17 of the Act. According to rule 43 the Revenue-officer is required to prepare compensation assessment rolls on the basis of the record-of-rights finally published or deemed to have been finally published under Chapter II of the Act. Rule 61 speaks about assignment of Touzi number under section 46(1). Rule 61 reads as follows:- 

 Rule 61 which speaks about the stage after the final publication of Compensation Assessment-rolls and the above noted provisions of the Act and other rules clearly show that the different classes of tenancies did not cease to exist immediately on the publication of the notification under section 3 of the Act; and the entire chain of rent-receivers would be eliminated only after the publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. Chapter XII of Part V provides about application of this part and class of agricultural tenants. Section 79 of Chapter XII speaks about commencement of Part V. It provides that Part V or any portion thereof shall come into force in such areas on such-dates and to such extent as the Government may, by notification, direct and when any portion of this Part comes into force in any area, the provisions of such portion shall have effect in such area notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. As section 79 provides Part V came into force in such areas, on such dates and to such extent as the Government by notification directed this notification of necessity was after publication of the notification under sub-section (2) of section 43 of the Act. Part V came into force in different areas on different dates by different notifications, Section 80 deals with repeal of the enactments specified in the schedule to the Act. Section 81 deals with agricultural tenants and regulation of their rights and liabilities. This section provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this Part in any area there shall, within that area, be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely. 'Malik’s," and the rights and liabilities of every such land-holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part. Section 81 A deals with rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants. Sub-section (1) of section 81 A provides that except as otherwise provided in this Part the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land who has become a tenant under the Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 applied to such land at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act, Section 82 provides the relevant interpretations. 

 11. Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, in support of the proposition that the under-raiyati of Ayesha Khatun became upgraded and formed a separate independent bolding, relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Anwara Begum v. Nurjahan, 27 DLR(AD) 109. From the reported decision it appears that similar question was under consideration on almost similar facts. Two applications under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act were filed in the Court of the Munsif at North Rauzan, Chittagong for pre-emption of transfer of certain land to the preemptee, claiming to be co-sharers in the occupancy raiyati holding to which the said land appertained. The pre-emption cases were contested by the pre-emptee contending, inter alia, that the land sought to be pre-empted appertained to korfa (under-raiyati) holding and as such right of pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not available to a co-sharer in the raiyati holding. The trial Court on evidence found that the holding was an occupancy raiyati holding and accordingly the pre-emption cases were allowed. On appeal the learned District Judge set aside the judgment and dismissed the pre-emption cases on the finding that the holding was a Korfa (under raiyati) holding without occupancy right and that pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not available. The learned Single Judge of the High Court however, reversed the decision on taking the view that the Korfa (under raiyati) was upgraded to a raiyati tenancy since14-4-56 as the rent receiving interest of the immediate landlord, this case a raiyat, stood acquired with effect from 14-4-56 under the general notification under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He allowed the revision cases and restored the judgments of the trial Court. 

 12. On the prayer of the pre-emptee leave was granted to consider (1) whether prior to coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act), the Korfa (under raiyati) tenancy became upgraded to a raiyati tenancy on and from 14-4-56 simply because by the general Notification under- section 3 of the Act the rent-receiving interests stood acquired with effect from 14-4-56; and (2) whether, in case of upgrading of under-raiyati to a raiyati in the above circumstances, pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was available in the instant case. 

 13. On behalf of the appellant it was argued that although on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest of the raiyat the under raiyati attached the status of a raiyat, but until Part V of the Act came into operation, the Bengal Ten any Act held the field, and as such a co-sharer in the raiyati holding could not maintain his application under section 26F for preemption of the transfer of the land appertaining to an under-raiyati holding. On behalf of the responder was argued that on the elimination of raiyati interest (rent-receiving) the under taiyati having been upgraded and attained the status of a raiyat, the application for pre-emption was maintainable. In support of his argument the learned Advocate referred to the decision in the case of Mobasher Ali V. Makbul Hossain. It appears that the appeal was dismissed with the following observation; 

 "Having considered the contention of the learned Counsel with reference to the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as well as the relevant provisions of the B.T. Act, we are inclined to hold that the view expressed in the case of Mubasher Ali that after the Notification issued under section 3 of the Act, the status of the under-raiyat became upgraded to that of raiyat, was correct and the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge of the High Court, being passed upon that view, calls for no interference.'' 

 (a) Whether before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation the under-raiyati, 'although his liability to pay rent direct to the Government commenced from. 14.4.56, became a raiyat or Malik under the Government as contemplated in section 81 of the Act; and 

 (b) whether section 3 (4) (e) read with section 81 support the contention that on the publication of Notification under section 3 the classification of the tenants made under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared •and all tenants attained the status of raiyats. 

 Chapter XII of Part V contains the heading "Application of this Part and class of agricultural tenants." Section 79 provides that Part V or any portion thereon shall come into force only by a notification published in the Official Gazette. Section 80 provides that with the notification the enactments specified in the schedule shall be repealed. According to this section Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed when Part V of the Act came into operation on the publication of the statutory notification in the Official Gazette, and this was done by separate notifications for separate are is of districts on different dates. The expression "there shall be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, Malik’s", as occurring in section 81 clearly implies that the existing classification of tenants will continue as such till Part V of the Act comes into force. Sections 79, 80 and 81 clearly show that from the date mentioned in the notification there shall be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, 'mans', and the rights and liabilities of every such holder shall be regulated by Part V. It also impliedly shows that till V came into operation some of the rights and liabilities of holders of agricultural land were being governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act. 

 15. (c) In the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 109 another relevant question was raised; namely, whether an under-raiyat becoming a tenant direct under the Government on the publication of the Notification under section 3, acquired the status of an occupancy raiyat as contemplated under the Bengal Tenancy Act, which was necessary for determination of the claim of pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. An application for pre-emption under section 26F by such a tenant or against such a tenant cannot be decided without a finding regarding the status of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee. Section 26F provides that in all cases of transfer of occupancy holding in raiyat land, whether by private sale or by sale in execution of a decree, or by foreclosure, a co-sharer in the holding shall have the right of pre-emption. In an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act one of the statutory requirements is that transfer sought to be pre-empted must to an occupancy holding. For successfully maintaining a case of pre-emption under section 26F it must be shown that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the holding with occupancy right ; and that transfer sought to be pre-empted is in respect of a part of an occupancy holding. The judgment does not show that this vital aspect of the case was examined. 

 16. All that sub-section (4)(e) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides is that all tenants holding lands in such estates (rent-receiving) shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate to the Government and not to anybody else. This speaks about the tenant's liability to pay rent the tenant is directed to pay rent to the Government directly and to nobody else. There is nothing in the statute that with the elimination of the rent-receiving interests a non-occupancy holding shall automatically stand raised to the class of occupancy holding. Chapter XIII deals with the incidents of holdings raiyats. Section 83 provides that a raiyat shall have the right to occupy and use the land comprised in his holding in any manner he likes. This Chapter makes it clear that before the publication of notification under section 80 an under-raiyat although treated as a raiyat under the Government for the purpose of realization of rent, such holding did not acquire the status of occupancy holding. With due respect to the learned Judges I must say that the conclusions arrived at in that case are not based on correct interpretation of the different provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder; and it does not provide the necessary guidance. 

 17. In my opinion after the Notification under section 3 and until Part V of the Act was brought into, operation, the classification of tenants as contemplated under section 4of the Bengal Tenancy Act continued; and with the publication of notification under section 80 the classifications and gradation of tenants disappeared and then all tenants became 'raiyats' or' Malik’s' under the Government; and further, only after such notification their rights and liabilities were to be governed under Part V.

Hassan and Sekandar Ali J.J. differed on this question.  Sekandar Ali, J" however on analysis of different provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, relevant for consideration of the question, did not find anything to change his view taken in the case of Manindra Chandra Ghose v. From the judgment it appears that the learned Judge while considering whether the Legislature in using the expression 'non-agricultural land' in sub-section (1) of section 24 used in the sense as 'holding' occurring in section 26F ofthe Bengal Tenancy Act added one further reason saying that section 24 entitles the immediate landlord to apply for preemption, and "the basis of such an application shall obviously be the individual character of the tenancy or jama." The learned Judge observed:- 

 "It will be no answer to such a claim' that the lands of the tenancy have been divided or partitioned amongst the tenants inter se, In other words; the landlord, if not otherwise ineligible will be entitled to pre-emption, regardless of any such division or partition "to which he is not a party. In my opinion it would be extremely anomalous to hold that the landlord is entitled to preemption inasmuch as the division or partition made by the tenants amongst themselves has not affected the undivided character of the tenancy and at the same time reject the application of she co-sharer tenant on the ground that by reason of the said division or partition he has ceased to have any connection with the particular land transferred or the parcel to which she land appertains." 

 "The expression 'tenant,' of necessity, pre-supposes a tenancy and the tenancy covers the entire land in respect of which the said tenancy was originally created unless the tenancy and the land were divided with the consent of the landlord. The tenancy and the entire land must be viewed as a unit and, as a whole, until such division or splitting up of the tenancy. There is, therefore, no magic in the word 'holding' as used in the Bengal Tenancy Act." 

 "It is obvious from the phraseology of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act that a right of pre-emption similar to that conferred by section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was intended to be given to co-tenants under the said section 24. What is required is the sharing of the tenancy itself and, furthermore, the tenancy must relate to the land in question." 

 "It is true that the petitioner-appellants are not co-possessors of the disputed land in the sense that they do not physically possess same. But, the portion of the land possessed by them upon mutual partition forms part of the same tenancy under which the disputed land was possessed by the predecessors of the respondents." 

 "Therefore, the tenancy is one and the land possessed by the petitioner-appellants and that possessed by the respondents form one unit under the said tenancy."

D)." 

 30. So far as the above noted conclusion is concerned, there is no dispute that the similar conclusion also flows from the facts of the case. In this case also by effecting partition on the basis of a decree of the Civil Court the co-sharers, namely, Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik a fid Rangubala Choudhurani possessed separately the land in their respective share, but the tenancy with the jama of Rs. 10/- was not divided or split up. It appears that the conclusion arrived at by Murshed, J., was considerably influenced by the fact that the jama continued as before. The learned Judge also noticed that the co-sharers after partition still continued to be co-sharer in the tenancy and their liability for payment of the rent continued as before although, as the learned Judge noticed, they ceased to be co-sharers in the land possessed by them separately. The learned Judge was also influenced by the consideration that section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as it stood then allowed the right to the immediate landlord of such non-agricultural tenant to pre-empt the transfer of a portion or share of the non-agricultural land. Sub-section (1) of section-24 was substituted by a new provision by East Pakistan Ordinance No. IX of 1967; one of the changes brought in was, the provision enabling the landlord to apply for pre-emption in the case of transfer of a portion or share of the non-agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant, was omitted from the statute. One of the reasons advanced by Sekandar Ali, J. was that the right of pre-emption could not be granted to the immediate landlord of the tenancy unless non-agricultural land was treated, synonymous to a tenancy. Murshed, J. agreeing with the above view of Sekandar Ali, J., held, that the petitioner appellants (pre-emptors) being co-sharer in the tenancy were also co-sharer in the land which is subject matter of the pre-emption case. In my opinion, the different provisions of section 24 do not warrant such a conclusion. Hassan J., noticed that the Legislature used the word 'tenancy' in some of the sections of the Act including sub-sections (7) and (11) of section 24 itself, while using the expression 'non-agricultural land' in sub-section (1); and the learned Judge also noticed that section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act speaks of transfer of a portion of a tenancy, whereas section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act does not speak of a tenancy, but of non-agricultural land though many other definitions have been quoted verbatimfrom section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The learned Judge made the following observation:— 

 "From the above it is clear that the Legislature has maintained a distinction between non-agricultural land and holding with a purpose; it may he to limit the number of applicants by making it available only to the co-sharers of the land and not of the tenancy, so that distribution amongst, all the co-sharers of the tenancy may not make the land unfit for the purpose for which it was taken. So, according to me, the words 'non-agricultural land' means a piece of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form the tenancy or a portion of tenancy. This interpretation will not throw the land open to the unlimited number of persons but to persons who are co-sharer-tenants under the same landlord in respect of undivided land though such co sharer-tenants may be co-sharer-tenants of the tenancy." 

 On careful consideration of the different sections of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and particularly different sub-sections of section 24 of the Act, I find myself in full agreement with the view expressed by Hasan, J. 

 31. In my opinion the Legislature consciously used the expression 'non-agricultural land' in sub-section (1) instead of using the expression 'tenancy' or 'holding' as used in sec. 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Trie Legislature does not use a word or expression in the statute unnecessarily. The Legislature being fully conscious about the object of the legislation, knew it better which particular word or expression would serve the purpose of the legislation. The different sub-sections of section 24 show that while mentioning the expression 'non-agricultural land Legislature used the word 'tenancy' in t provision to sub-section (7) and sub-section (1) of section 24. The word 'tenancy' used in some of the sub-sections of -section 24 as noticed above, lends support to the argument that the legislature was not unmindful of the word 'tenancy' while using the expression "non- agricultural land" in different sub-sections of section 24; and it consciously did not use the word tenancy In sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Act. While examining the different provisions of section 24 it strikes me that the provision of pre-emption as contained in section 24 shall not apply to transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase. Sub-section (11), clause (a) of section 24 read as under:— 

 (a) a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose existing interest has accrued other-wise than by purchase." 

 If the above provision- in sub-section (11), clause (a) is read along with sub-section (1) of section 24 the intention of the Legislature in not using the word 'tenancy' in sub-section (1), becomes clear. It appears that the Legislature has maintained a distinction between the expressions 'non-agricultural land' and 'holding' with a purpose, which may be to limit the number of applicants by making it available only to the co-sharers of the land and not to co-sharers in the tenancy, so that the distribution among all the co-sharers may not make the land unfit for the purpose for which it is taken. It is a matter of common experience that in the town or city how the 'non-agricultural land' is owned by more than one co-sharer in the tenancy. 'Non-agricultural tenant' as defined in section 2(5) clearly indicates the nature, of its use. A non-agricultural tenant' holds non-agricultural land for- 

 32. The nature of non-agricultural land by non-agricultural tenant as shown in the definitions, and use of the expression 'non- agricultural land' in sub-section (1) of section 24 instead of using the expression 'non-agricultural tenancy', sufficiently indicate why the Legislature used the expression 'non-agricultural land' in section 24. It obviously shows that the purpose is to keep number of pre-emptors limited to the co-sharers in the land, so that the land on pre-emption may not become unfit for use. For clarification of the point let me cite an illustration. A non-agricultural tenancy holding on partition is being owned and possessed separately by say, three co-sharers, and the co-sharer owners thereof by constructing their respective houses are living there and the three houses have been registered as separate holdings under the Municipal Act, but jama of the tenancy remaining undivided; consequently their liability to pay rent to the immediate landlord also remains joint. There is nothing common amongst Ute co-sharer tenants excepting their joint liability in the matter of payment of rent; and they ceased to be co-sharers for all practical purposes. Now, if a portion or share of the land held on partition, is transferred to a stranger, and pre-emption is made open to all the co-sharers in the tenancy, namely, if all owners of three holdings are allowed pre-emption, the result may not be at all enviable because, as a result of distribution of the land amongst all the co-tenants of the tenancy, there is the possibility that on distribution the parcels of land becoming unfit for use. To avoid this consequence, it would not be unreasonable to think that the Legislature consciously used the expression 'co-sharer in the land' instead of using the expression co-sharer in tenancy. That the Legislature used the expression 'co-sharer in the land' in sub-sec. (1) of section 24 consciously becomes also clear from the scheme of the Act. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has recognized 'non-agricultural land' as an entity or unit separate from non- agricultural tenancy', because, both the expressions have been used in different sections to suit the purpose of the legislation. Before amendment of section 24 right of pre-emption provided therein was of two categories, namely, 

 33. By amendment right of pre-emption allowed to the immediate landlord has been omitted. So, section 24 after amendment provides right of pre-emption only to the co-sharer tenants in the land. In allowing pre-emption the expression 'co-sharer tenant in the land' has been used in sub- section (1) of section 24, but in clause (a) of sub-section (11) of section 24 protecting from pre-emption a transfer of a portion of the land to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase, the expression 'co-sharer in the tenancy' has been used. Clause (a) of sub-section (11) provides that nothing in this section shall apply to-"a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase." The above provisions sufficiently indicate intention of the Legislature in using the expression 'a co-sharer in the tenancy' and 'a co-sharer in the land' in different sections of the Act. Transfer of a portion or share of the 'non-agriculture land' to a stranger opens right of pre-emption to one or more co-sharer tenants of such land but when a portion or share of non-agricultural landis transferred to a co-sharer in the tenancy this is protected. The relationship of land- lord and tenant and incidents of tenant's holdings as evident from Chapters III and IV of the Act, show that both the expressions have been conveniently used to suit the purpose of the legislation. The scheme of the Bengal Tenancy Act shows that conveniences of cultivation received upper consideration of the Legislature but in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the Legislature is primarily concerned with the consideration of convenience of tenants' residence. In the Bengal Tenancy Act in in enumerating the rights and liabilities of the tenants vis-a-vis the rights and obligations of the landlords, 'tenancy' has been used, but in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in this respect while using the expression non-agricultural tenancy' the expression 'non-agricultural land' has also been used. Under the Bengal Tenancy Act a suit for ejectment is filed on the basis of the tenancy and all the co-sharers in the tenancy are to be impleaded in the suit. Bengal Tenancy Act does not provide for successfully proceeding against some of the tenants in relation to a portion of the tenancy. A suit for ejectment of one or more tenants without impleading all the tenants in the tenancy is liable to fail. But the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act provides that a landlord may proceed against some of the tenants occupying a parcel or portion of the tenancy instead of proceeding against all of them. Section 70 reads as under:- 

 "No non- agricultural tenant shall be ejected from the tenancy or from any non-agricultural land which he holds except in execution of a decree of a competent Civil Court." 

 This provision provides the complete answer to the controversy as to whether the expressions 'non-agricultural tenancy' and 'non-agricultural land' carry the same sense. Section 70 provides the option to the landlord to choose as to whether the suit for ejectment should be filed in respect of the tenancy or a part of the tenancy, 

 34. In view of what has been stated above, in my opinion the respondents not being co-sharer in the land transferred, though they may be co-sharer in the tenancy, the right of pre-emption did not accrue in their favour and as such their application for pre-emption must fail.

The judgments of the Courts below allowing pre-emption in favour of the respondents, and that of the High Court Division affirming the same, are set aside and the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act filed by the respondents is dismissed.

The learned Single Judge disagreeing with the trial Court and the lower appellate court held that under raiyati was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun, but on the acquisition of rent receiving interest of Rangubala, the under raiyati was upgraded to a raiyati directly under the Government whereupon Respondent No. 1 and the appellant became co- sharers again as raiyats in the same tenancy. 

 40. The main ground urged before us by Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellant, is that the upgrading of the under-raiyati no doubt took place on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interests on April 14, 1956, but this upgrading did not re unite the former under-raiyati with the one- third share of the original tenancy which also became a raiyati under the Government. The upgrading of this under-raiyati resulted in creation of a separate, distinct and independent raiyati having no connection with the raiyati of Nafisa Khatun, vendor of Respondent No.1. In other words, on this 'upgrading' the former share of Nafisa and i share of Rangubala became two independent tenancies. Mr. M. H. Khandkar, learned Advocate for the Respondent contends that the finding of the learned Single Judge that an under-raiyati was created by the Lease Deed is erroneous since the S.A. Khatian did not support the creation of any under-raiyati and the original jama of Rs. 10/- for the entire tenancy also continued to be paid. But it should be noted that presumptive value of record of rights prepared under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not attached to a S.A. khatian. Secondly, though the original jama was shown in the S.A. khatian, Respondent No. 1 could not produce any rent receipt for payment of rent at the original rate. Appellant, on the other hand produced rent-receipts showing that Ayesha paid rent to Rangubala and thereafter to the Government in respect of the  share of the former tenancy. As to the Lease-Deed, it is a registered instrument expressly creating a lease under Rangubala. As such I do not find any substance in the contention that no under-raiyati was created. 

 41. Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the 1/3rd share of Akshoy became a co-sharer of Rangubala in the original tenancy but she did not become a co-sharer of Ayesha as Ayesha's interest was an under-raiyati under Rangubala-who was in fact her (Nafisa) co-sharer. This is because, after creating an under raiyati under her Rangubala herself did not become a co-sharer of her tenant, Ayesha, A person who takes lease in respect of a portion of a land of which the other portion is held by the lessor, the former does not become a co-sharer within the meaning of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. This view taken by the learned Single Judge of the then High Court in the case of Manindra Chandra Ghosh V. Mujibul Islam, 12 DLR 785 on which Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed relies is found to be correct for the simple reason that a lessor and his lessee cannot be co-sharers in the same tenancy. The original tenancy, on the creation of the lease stands divided. This was the position in respect of Ayesha Khatun' sunder-raiyat till the acquisition of the rent-receiving interests on "14 April 1956, when Rangubala, along with her superior interests, disappeared from the scene altogether, and consequently, the under-raiyat rose up and became araiyat directly under the Government. This upgrading took place by operation of Jaw) namely, section 3(4)(e) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950. This provides that on the acquisition of rent- receiving interests all tenants holding land in' estates, tenures holdings directly under a rent-receiver become tenants directly under the Government. Effect of this 'upgrading' is same as the merger of interests of a landlord with that of his raiyat under section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as it stood amended in 1907. Section 22 provides that when the superior landlord purchases an occupancy-holding under him, the holding itself disappears and consequently the status of an under-raiyat is raised to that of a raiyat. The logic behind this merger is that when a landlord purchases a raiyat holding in execution of a rent decree he shall hold the land not as a raiyat but as a land-lord such as a proprietor or tenure-holder, and the under-raiyati created by the outgoing raiyat not being annulled at the option of the landlord the under raiyat takes the position of the raiyat. In the instant case, after disappearance of all classes of rent receivers, only one class of tenants remained in the field paying rent directly to the Government. In the instant case Ayesha Khatun became a tenant directly under the Government with effect from 15-4-1956. It is true that Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into operation on a much later date. 1962, but during this intervening period, only one class of tenants remained on the land paying rent direct to the government. Retention of different classes of tenants in the record of rights, prepared or revised under Chapter IV of this Act, was intended for completing some consequential work such as realization of arrears of rent at different rates existing at the time of the acquisition, payment of rent to the government at the existing rates, payment of compensation tothe ex-rent-receivers. During this period payment of rent to any person other than government as well as sub-letting of land was totally prohibited. As such, retention of the former classification of tenants in record of rights did not stand in the way of automatic creation of only one class of tenants. In the case of "Mobasher Ali v. Mokbul Hossain;" 19 DLR, 271 a Division Bench of the High Court, on examining all previous decisions on this point took a similar view which was approved and confirmed by the Appellate Division in the case of Anwara Begum Vs. Nurjahan, 27 DLR (AD) 109. Again, in the instant case, the date of upgrading of the under-raiyati into a raiyati is not material. As such, I see no ground to take a different view about the date of the statutory upgrading of the status of under-raiyats. 

 42. The crucial question in this case is whether the upgrading of Ayesha Khatun's under-raiyati made her a co-sharer with Nafisa Khatun, vendor of the preemptor, or whether this up-grading resulted in effecting two separate tenancies, each independent of the other, one in respect of the former 2/3 share of Rangubala and the other in respect of the former 1/3rd share of Akshoy in the original tenancy. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division relying upon a decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Anwara Begum, 27 DLR (AD) 109 as already referred to, has held that because of die "upgrading" Ayesha Khatun became a co-sharer of Nafisa Khatun in the original' tenancy and consequently, Nafisa Khatun's transferee, namely the pre-emptor became a co sharer therein. But if the relationship in the same tenancy bad been snapped in the year 1953 by creation of the under-raiyati, how the two separate tenancies could be united into one tenancy by the subsequent upgrading? In the case of Mubasher Ali (19 DLR 271) the High Court simply approved of the principle of "upgrading", but did not decide the question whether such "upgrading" led to re-unification of the former under- raiyati and the raiyati into a single tenancy but left the question open to be decided after the remand which was directed. The Division Bench in that case accepted the contention raised by the preempted that: in spite of the raising of his status an under- raiyat could claim a separate tenancy in respect of his share. In a previous case, I Rafiqul Islam Vs. Taibur Rahman', 18 DLR 475 exactly on this very question, the High Court took the view that by 'upgrading', the former separate tenancies are not re united into a single tenancy. The view taken in that case is quoted: 

 This decision is not found to have been cited in the case of Anwara Begum, 27 DLR (AD) 109. The principle of law on this subject is that where an under-raiyati is created by a raiyat, the latter is not a co-sharer of the former; and when the superior interest of the raiyat is extinguished and he disappears, the under-raiyat is upgraded into a raiyat but only in respect of his own share. If the previous "raiyat or for that matter his co-sharer raiyat held khas any portion of the original tenancy, that portion becomes a separate raiyati under the government with which the upgraded raiyat bas got no connection. Inview of this position the under-raiyati held by Ayesha upgraded into an independent raiyati which got no connection with the raiyati previously held by Nafisa, now by Respondent No. 1. As such Respondent No. 1 is not a co-sharer of the appellant and he got no right to pre-empt the land purchased by the appellant from Ayesha Khatun. I would, therefore, accept Ground No. 1 of Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed which is alone sufficient to the dispose of this appeal. 

 43. In view of this position, the other ground of Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed—which is rather an alternative ground—need not be considered. But it may be mentioned that by a decree in a partition suit the parties go into separate and exclusive possession of their respective shares in the land of a holding, but such a decree does not result in the splitting up of holding along with its jama which may be done only by subdivision of the holding under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, corresponding to section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Right of pre-emption is not extinguished by partition as was rightly held in the case of Md. Shukura Vs. Ram Chandra Kapali 6 DLR, 393. This principle however will apply only in the case of a "holding". Whether this principle will be applicable in the case of a non-agricultural tenancy will depend upon the question whether "Non-agricultural land" under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the "holding" under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, corresponding to section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, are synonymous carrying the same meaning. The learned Counsel has submitted that success of this alternative ground—that these two terms are not synonymous—will not help his case nor its failure will harm it. Secondly, a Full Bench of the High Court in the case of "Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury V. Rezia Begum", 16 DLR 77 examined this question and by majority decision held that these two terms, "non-agricultural land" and "holding" are synonymous carrying the same meaning. Since this question is not necessary for disposal of the instant appeal, I would refrain-from expressing any opinion as to the correctness of the decision of the High Court in that case. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost, the orders allowing pre-emption are set aside and the application for pre-emption is dismissed.
